newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African minister warns WTO may become elitist.
newsitem.headline: S.African minister warns WTO may become elitist.

text.p: South Africa's trade and industry minister Alec Erwin on Thursday called for greater co-operation to stop the World Trade Organisation (WTO) from becoming an elitist body.

Erwin said the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), of which South Africa is president, had made moves to enhance dialogue and understanding between emerging nations and more developed states.

"It is South Africa's submission that it is not UNCTAD alone that has to make this change. It is a challenge for all multilateral organisations," Erwin said in a speech delivered at the WTO's first ministerial meeting in Singapore and released in South Africa.
Erwin said world trade was still dominated by a handful of major nations such as the United States, Japan and those of the European Union.
"The question that arises out of this quantitive domination of trade by relatively few countries is whether there is a risk of the WTO becoming a de facto select group," he said.
"This must not be allowed to happen," he added.

Erwin said the globalisation of the world economy offered potential for developing emerging markets as well as a risk of marginalising many poorer countries. This dilemma could only be solved by cooperation between the world's have and have-nots.
"We will not do this if our multi-lateral organisations, working in their clearly defined areas of competence, don't work together," he said.
Erwin warned that there was a risk of UNCTAD becoming a haven for the developing world while the WTO fell into the hands of the developed nations.
"If the WTO becomes the terrain of the strong and UNCTAD the defensive shield of the weak then, we destroy a partnership for growth, development and trade," he said.
But he called on developing countries to form their own economic partnership zones in order to woo much-needed foreign direct investment (FDI).
"It would seem that to enhance FDI flows, the message is clear -- developing countries must form their own economic zones," he said.
Erwin attacked the developed world for trying to bully poorer countries into wide-ranging reforms, while making few changes themselves.

"It is self-seeking and ultimately short-sighted for the developed countries to plead all sorts of technical and political reasons for not dismantling agricultrue subsidies or failing to ratify labour standards, yet ask the developing world to agree to multilateral agreements that require far greater socio-economic and political change," he said.
